fields.priorText: The Christian God best unifies contingent reality, objective normativity, and the earliest resurrection testimony when rival explanations are compared.
Changing and contingent realities require a ground that is neither merely another dependent item nor an unexplained member of the same series.
A necessary ground without unrealized potential can be immaterial and causally basic, although each additional divine attribute requires an explicit bridge.
Objective moral obligations favor a perfectly good personal ground if secular accounts cannot explain their binding authority and universality.
Resurrection evidence requires comparative testing of early testimony, group reports, empty-tomb traditions, source dependence, and plausible natural alternatives.
If resurrection remains the best explanation after those comparisons, it identifies the metaphysical ground with the God proclaimed by earliest Christianity.
Christian theism gains support when its metaphysical, moral, and historical explanations jointly outperform their strongest naturalistic and textual alternatives.

One necessary cause should explain several domains rather than operate as an isolated exception. If the same account explains contingent existence, rational order, moral authority, and resurrection belief with fewer independent assumptions than rival accounts, cumulative force exceeds any single analogy. The comparison must still count the explanatory costs of divine attributes and difficult scripture.

Hiddenness may reflect tension between evidence sufficient for responsible inquiry and evidence so immediate that deliberation changes character. This defense needs predictions about where sincere nonbelief remains possible and where accessible evidence should appear. Those predictions can be compared with persistent disagreement, religious experience, moral transformation, and unanswered prayer instead of appealing without limit to unknown reasons.

Place every retained datum against bodily resurrection, private grief, legendary growth, mistaken burial, and visionary appearances. Test each rival against women at the tomb, named and group reports, Paul’s hostility, narrative variation, and source dependence. A transparent matrix prevents one favored datum from carrying the inference and reveals which account leaves the fewest serious residues.
The Christian God remains insufficiently supported when divine predictions, scriptural morality, and resurrection evidence are no better explained than natural alternatives.
A God claimed to act through prayer and revelation should generate publicly discriminating outcomes beyond ordinary chance, psychology, and institutional behavior.
The observed distribution of suffering and unanswered prayer counts against protective intervention unless the relevant expectations are independently qualified.
Scriptural violence challenges perfect goodness when literal divine attribution survives genre analysis and compensation cannot justify choosing harmful means.
Resurrection testimony loses force when source dependence, material conflicts, visionary readings, and natural grief experiences remain live alternatives.
Metaphysical arguments do not establish Christianity unless necessity principles are defended and inferred attributes connect independently to specifically Christian claims.
Withholding belief is justified when the Christian hypothesis does not produce a clearer and better-supported total explanation than naturalistic competitors.

Translate theological claims into predictions before examining outcomes. Answered prayer, institutional guidance, and loving revelation should imply specified patterns, while permissible divine silence must be bounded rather than invoked after each failure. Recording expected successes, allowed failures, and comparison baselines turns Barker’s testing intuition into disciplined evidence and shows which claims genuinely risk disconfirmation.

Future compensation concerns whether victims eventually flourish, not whether an agent was justified in choosing lethal or traumatic means. The moral challenge should separate restoration from necessity, proportionality, consent, and available alternatives. Even granting eternal life, perfect power appears to widen the range of less harmful means, so the defense must explain why violence was required rather than merely repairable.

Narrative agreement supports resurrection only when accounts provide independent access rather than repeat shared traditions. Separate common-source agreement, independent attestation, and later elaboration, then test whether differences reflect perspective or incompatible development. This improves on listing contradictions because it connects textual relationships directly to evidential weight and rival historical explanations.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The existence of God is a philosophical rather than a scientific question.
moves.warrant: Science supplies natural explanations for observable phenomena but does not by itself settle immaterial realities such as minds, moral truths, free will, or God.
moves.inference: The audience should assess philosophical arguments directly rather than require a scientific consensus or laboratory result.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But before I present my evidence, let me point out that we are not discussing a scientific question. Science provides natural explanations for observable phenomena in the universe. Science can never answer philosophical questions about the existence of immaterial things like moral truths, minds, abstract objects, free will, or God. Philosophers are divided, sometimes evenly, about these issues. So we can't point to a consensus like we do in science. Instead, we have to look at the arguments for ourselves and make up our own minds.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe's finite past requires an uncaused, timeless, immaterial, powerful personal cause.
moves.warrant: An actually traversed infinite series of past events would never reach today; a beginning requires a cause beyond space and time, and an immaterial chooser rather than an abstract object can initiate a temporal universe.
moves.inference: A cause bearing central divine attributes exists.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Here's the argument from First Cause. In his book, Godless, Dan says God could never finish the infinite series of thoughts in his mind before saying, let there be light. What Dan fails to appreciate, however, is that God's mind isn't fragmented into an infinite series of mental events. God is an infinite, undivided act of being who knows everything in one timeless act of existence. But Dan is right that if God had to traverse an infinite number of thoughts, he could never get anything done. Similarly, if time had to traverse an infinite number of events before today, then today would never happen. But today did happen. Therefore, the past is finite and had a beginning. And if the universe had a beginning, then it had a cause to explain why it began to exist. Most atheists believe that if prayer healed an amputated limb, that would be a miracle. But if the universe came into existence from nothing, wouldn't that also be a miracle? If the universe includes all space and time, then the cause of the universe must exist beyond space and time, and be uncaused, or the argument starts all over again. It must be all-powerful because it made something from nothing. And it must be personal because this timeless cause chose to create a finite, temporal universe, and the only kinds of immaterial entities that exist are minds and abstract objects, the latter of which can't cause anything. Therefore, the cause of the universe's beginning must be an immaterial, eternal, all-powerful agent, or what most people call God.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Present change requires a first actualizer that is pure actuality and possesses divine attributes.
moves.warrant: Potentials are actualized by something actual; an infinite instrumental series no more explains current change than infinitely many train cars explain motion without a locomotive, so the terminus has no unrealized potential.
moves.inference: An immaterial, timeless, necessary, powerful, knowing, and good actualizer exists even if the universe is temporally eternal.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The argument from motion. Things change, that's obvious. And change is just the reduction of a potential to an actual. For example, a train car can potentially go down a track, but that potential to move can only be actualized by something else pulling the car down the track. And whatever is pulling the car has to be pulled by something else, because nothing can actualize its own potential, any more than it could create itself from nothing. But maybe the universe's motion and change have existed forever. That would be like saying a train car is moving because an infinite number of cars is pulling it, or that a paintbrush could paint by itself as long as it had an infinitely long handle. An infinite series of movers doesn't explain why there's any motion at all, be it in a train or a universe. The train only moves because of something that gives motion, but doesn't receive it, like a locomotive. Likewise, our universe only has motion and change because of something that actualizes the potential in all objects, but has no potential of its own, and is just pure actuality. So what is this first mover or changer like? Well, if it has no potential, then it can't potentially go out of existence, or potentially increase in ability. So it must be infinite and necessary. It can't be material or temporal, because that would entail the potential to move and change. So it must be immaterial and timeless. It must be all-powerful, because there is no potential act it can't perform. It must be all-knowing, because it provides actual existence to potential properties and relations between objects, which are the basic elements of knowledge. Finally, this cause has to be all-good, because evil is just a lack of good, and the ultimate cause has no potentials or deficiencies. An infinite necessary... immaterial, timeless, all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good being is what people mean by the word God.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe's contingent existence is explained by a necessary being rather than by nothing or an infinite series of dependent universes.
moves.warrant: Brute existence would undermine ordinary explanatory practice, the universe does not exist by definition, and adding dependent universes never supplies a nondependent explanation.
moves.inference: A necessary being of pure actuality explains why anything exists.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The argument from existence. Why is there something rather than nothing? There are only three explanations for why the universe exists at all. It exists for no reason, the universe is necessary, or it has to exist, or three, the universe is explained by something that is not the universe. Number one doesn't work because if things could exist for no reason, then we would expect to see objects like cats or chrysalers popping into existence all the time for no reason. Science also functions on the principle that unexplained phenomena have an explanation even if we don't know what it is yet. Number two doesn't work because the universe is not necessary. You might ask why a triangle is lime green, but you wouldn't ask why it's three-sided. A triangle just has to be three-sided. But the question why does the universe exist isn't like asking why is a triangle three-sided. The answer isn't obvious because the universe doesn't have to exist, it just does exist, and that requires an explanation. But the explanation of the universe can't be dependent on other things to exist, like say another universe, because it too would need to be explained. If an infinite number of universes doesn't explain why all these universes exist, any more than an infinitely long chain unattached to a ceiling explains what is holding a chandelier over our heads. Instead, there must be a necessary being, and since I've shown a being of pure actuality is necessary because it has no potentials of any kind, and thus it has to exist, this provides another reason to believe that a cause with divine attributes, or God, exists.

moves.claim: Jesus' bodily resurrection is the best explanation of early Christian testimony and the empty-tomb tradition.
moves.warrant: Paul reports individual, group, and skeptical witnesses; Jewish expectations disfavored a resurrected failed messiah; group experience, Paul's prior hostility, access to a Jerusalem tomb, and women as discoverers are offered against hallucination or invention.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But how do we know this God is the Christian God? What if this cause is the God of another religion? The gods of ancient mythologies are limited in existence, goodness, power, and knowledge, so they can't be the true God. The true God could only be the God of classical monotheism, like Islam, Judaism, or Christianity. But if Jesus rose from the dead, then this shows the God of Christianity exists, because other religions deny Jesus rose from the dead. Antony Flew, who was at one time one of the most famous atheists in the 20th century, said the evidence for the resurrection is better than proclaimed miracles in any other religion. It's outstandingly different in quality and quantity. Even radical skeptics do not deny that Paul knew the apostles, and describe in 1 Corinthians 15 how both individuals and groups of people, as well as skeptics like himself, saw Jesus after his death. In addition, these first Christians believed Jesus rose from the dead in a Jewish society that believed dead messiahs were failed imposters, who, along with everyone else, would not rise until the end of the world. The best explanation for why Jesus' disciples preached Jesus' bodily resurrection, in defiance of these cultural norms, was because it really happened. But perhaps the apostles merely had a grief-induced hallucination. That's what Dan suggests in his writings. But there are four reasons that count against this hypothesis. One, groups of people saw Jesus, and groups of people don't have the exact same hallucination. Two, Paul was a persecutor of the church, so he would not have had any grief over the death of Jesus from which to hallucinate. Three, Jesus was buried in Jerusalem. The apostles could check his tomb to see if he really was dead, and the authorities could trot out his corpse in order to quash this new religious movement. Four, the apostles did check, and the tomb was empty. The gospel's descriptions of women discovering the empty tomb is a detail that is so embarrassing in a patriarchal society that its inclusion in the narrative only makes sense if that is just what really happened.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Dan also misunderstands the Bible's non-literal language. Psalm 91.4, for example, says that God will cover you with his feathers, but he's not a chicken. When we teach people about realities beyond their existence, you have to start with simple, non-literal explanations. For example, in introductory chemistry, electrons are described as tiny tennis balls that neatly orbit the nucleus of an atom. But that's not correct. They're actually chaotic clouds that don't have defined points. So in the same way, God is definitely a reality beyond our experience. So it's not surprising the Bible represents God coming down to our level and using simple, non-literal descriptions of himself so that ancient people could understand him. That means God's anger refers to how our sin separates us from God. And God's jealousy refers to how he is like a husband who is zealous to protect his wife. The Hebrew word rendered jealous, or khanah, even means zeal. It also means that descriptions of God lifting up skirts or making people eat their children aren't literal. They reflect a developing theology that did not distinguish between God directly causing evil and merely permitting it to happen. And so it was often conflated. That means God is not, as Dan says, a sadomasochistic, misogynistic bully. Moreover, the non-literal language can be seen in the alleged commands that Israel wipe out or utterly destroy the Canaanites. King Merneptah of Egypt used similar language to describe the complete destruction of Israel, even though Israel continued to exist for centuries after that point. So the language can be read to talk about radical separation, not extermination.

Resurrection evidence requires comparative testing of early testimony, group reports, empty-tomb traditions, source dependence, and plausible natural alternatives.
If resurrection remains the best explanation after those comparisons, it identifies the metaphysical ground with the God proclaimed by earliest Christianity.
finalArgument.conclusion: Christian theism gains support when its metaphysical, moral, and historical explanations jointly outperform their strongest naturalistic and textual alternatives.

newArguments.title: Unified Explanatory Economy
newArguments.text: One necessary cause should explain several domains rather than operate as an isolated exception. If the same account explains contingent existence, rational order, moral authority, and resurrection belief with fewer independent assumptions than rival accounts, cumulative force exceeds any single analogy. The comparison must still count the explanatory costs of divine attributes and difficult scripture.

newArguments.title: Calibrated Hiddenness
newArguments.text: Hiddenness may reflect tension between evidence sufficient for responsible inquiry and evidence so immediate that deliberation changes character. This defense needs predictions about where sincere nonbelief remains possible and where accessible evidence should appear. Those predictions can be compared with persistent disagreement, religious experience, moral transformation, and unanswered prayer instead of appealing without limit to unknown reasons.

newArguments.title: Resurrection Rival Matrix
newArguments.text: Place every retained datum against bodily resurrection, private grief, legendary growth, mistaken burial, and visionary appearances. Test each rival against women at the tomb, named and group reports, Paul’s hostility, narrative variation, and source dependence. A transparent matrix prevents one favored datum from carrying the inference and reveals which account leaves the fewest serious residues.

finalArgument.thesis: The Christian God remains insufficiently supported when divine predictions, scriptural morality, and resurrection evidence are no better explained than natural alternatives.
premises: A God claimed to act through prayer and revelation should generate publicly discriminating outcomes beyond ordinary chance, psychology, and institutional behavior.
The observed distribution of suffering and unanswered prayer counts against protective intervention unless the relevant expectations are independently qualified.
Scriptural violence challenges perfect goodness when literal divine attribution survives genre analysis and compensation cannot justify choosing harmful means.
Resurrection testimony loses force when source dependence, material conflicts, visionary readings, and natural grief experiences remain live alternatives.
Metaphysical arguments do not establish Christianity unless necessity principles are defended and inferred attributes connect independently to specifically Christian claims.
finalArgument.conclusion: Withholding belief is justified when the Christian hypothesis does not produce a clearer and better-supported total explanation than naturalistic competitors.

newArguments.title: Prediction Ledger
newArguments.text: Translate theological claims into predictions before examining outcomes. Answered prayer, institutional guidance, and loving revelation should imply specified patterns, while permissible divine silence must be bounded rather than invoked after each failure. Recording expected successes, allowed failures, and comparison baselines turns Barker’s testing intuition into disciplined evidence and shows which claims genuinely risk disconfirmation.

newArguments.title: Means Versus Compensation
newArguments.text: Future compensation concerns whether victims eventually flourish, not whether an agent was justified in choosing lethal or traumatic means. The moral challenge should separate restoration from necessity, proportionality, consent, and available alternatives. Even granting eternal life, perfect power appears to widen the range of less harmful means, so the defense must explain why violence was required rather than merely repairable.

newArguments.title: Source Dependence Test
newArguments.text: Narrative agreement supports resurrection only when accounts provide independent access rather than repeat shared traditions. Separate common-source agreement, independent attestation, and later elaboration, then test whether differences reflect perspective or incompatible development. This improves on listing contradictions because it connects textual relationships directly to evidential weight and rival historical explanations.
